etymology: Greek Maththias, from Hebrew Mattithyah, "gift of YHWH"; the disciple chosen by lot to replace Judas among the twelve apostles.
biblical_def: Matthias was the disciple chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles, restoring their number before Pentecost. In the days between the ascension and Pentecost, Peter stood among the gathered believers and explained from the Psalms that another must take the office Judas had forfeited (Acts 1:20). The qualification was specific: he must be one "which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us... a witness with us of his resurrection" (Acts 1:21-22). Two men met the standard: Joseph called Barsabbas, and Matthias. The believers prayed, asking the Lord who knows all hearts to show His choice, and cast lots; "and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles" (Acts 1:26). Of his later labors Scripture says nothing further; tradition holds he preached and was martyred. Matthias stands in the dictionary as the apostle chosen to complete the Twelve, a witness of the resurrection from the beginning, whose selection by prayer and lot shows the early church seeking the mind of the Lord, and whose quiet entrance into the apostolic college testifies that God knows and appoints His servants, even those Scripture names but once.
webster_summary: The disciple chosen by lot (Acts 1:23-26) to replace Judas among the twelve apostles; a witness of Christ's resurrection from John's baptism onward, selected after the believers prayed for the Lord to show His choice.

corruption_summary: Matthias's choosing honors the recovery of the apostolic qualification — eyewitness of the risen Christ — and of the church seeking God's choice in prayer, against a casual view of office and a doubt that questions God's ordering of His church.
corruption_paragraphs: Office-trivialized correction. The apostleship was no honorary title but a specific office requiring eyewitness testimony to the risen Christ. Matthias qualified because he had companied with the Lord from the beginning and seen Him risen. The dictionary holds that the foundational apostolic witness was grounded in eyewitness fact, not later invention; the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph 2:20), men who had seen the Lord and could testify of His resurrection.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is seeking the Lord's choice in prayer. The believers did not lobby or campaign but prayed, "Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen" (Acts 1:24). The dictionary commends their dependence: in the choosing of leaders the church is to seek the mind of the Lord who knows all hearts, trusting Him to appoint His own servants, as He appointed Matthias to complete the Twelve.

etymology: Greek Prochoros, "leader of the dance" or "before the chorus"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6.
biblical_def: Prochorus was one of the seven men chosen by the early Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution to the widows, freeing the apostles for prayer and the ministry of the Word. When a complaint arose that the Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the daily ministration, the apostles called the multitude and said, "It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables. Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business" (Acts 6:2-3). The church chose seven, including Stephen, Philip, and Prochorus, and the apostles prayed and laid hands on them. This appointment is widely regarded as the origin of the office of deacon, the servant-office given to the practical care of the church's needy. Of Prochorus himself Scripture records nothing beyond his name in the list; later tradition, of uncertain value, made him a companion of the apostle John. Prochorus stands in the dictionary as one of the first seven servants of the church, a witness to the institution of practical, merciful service as a holy office, and a reminder that the care of the church's needy is no lesser work, but a ministry for which men full of the Spirit and wisdom are required.
webster_summary: One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the widows and free the apostles for the Word; his appointment (with the others) marks the origin of the office of deacon, the church's servant-office of practical mercy.

corruption_summary: Prochorus and the Seven honor the recovery of the diaconate and the dignity of practical mercy-service, against a view that prizes only public ministry and despises the humble care of the needy.
corruption_paragraphs: Service-despised correction. The world, and sometimes the church, esteems only visible, prominent ministry and counts the practical care of the needy a lesser task. The Seven were chosen for exactly that practical service — yet the church required men "full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" for it. The dictionary holds that mercy-ministry is a holy office: those who serve the office of a deacon well purchase a good degree and great boldness in the faith (1 Tim 3:13), and the care of the church's poor is dear to her Lord.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wise ordering of ministry. The apostles refused to leave the Word to serve tables, not because tables did not matter, but because both ministries mattered and neither should be neglected. The dictionary commends the pattern: the church distributes its labors so that prayer and the Word are not crowded out and the needy are not overlooked, appointing Spirit-filled servants to each work that all may be done well.

etymology: Greek Nikanor, "conqueror"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6.
biblical_def: Nicanor was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution to the widows (Acts 6:5). Like his fellows, he is named only in the list of the Seven, yet his appointment is part of a passage rich in instruction about the qualifications for holy service. The apostles required that the men chosen be of "honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" (Acts 6:3) — a striking standard for what was, in essence, the administration of charity. The work of distributing food to widows did not call merely for honesty or organizational skill, but for men marked by a good reputation, filled with the Spirit, and possessed of practical wisdom. This teaches that even the most practical service in the church is a spiritual work, to be entrusted to spiritual men. The Greek names of the Seven (Nicanor among them) suggest they were Hellenists, chosen with sensitivity to heal the very division that had arisen between the Greek-speaking and Hebrew-speaking believers. Nicanor stands in the dictionary as one of the Seven, a witness that the church entrusts even its practical and material ministries to men of the Spirit, and that wise, godly administration is itself a gift and a calling within the body of Christ.
webster_summary: One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the widows; named only in the list, yet a witness that even practical, material ministry in the church requires men "of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom."

corruption_summary: Nicanor and the Seven honor the recovery of Spirit-filled wisdom in the church's practical administration, against a secular notion that material ministry needs only competence, not godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: Competence-only correction. A managerial age supposes that the practical affairs of the church need only skilled administrators, not spiritual men. The apostles thought otherwise, requiring that even the distributors of food to widows be full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom (Acts 6:3). The dictionary holds that all the church's work, material as well as spiritual, is to be done by godly people in dependence on the Spirit; competence without godliness is not the church's standard for any office.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is wise, reconciling administration. The Seven, bearing Greek names, were apparently chosen from the very Hellenist group that had felt neglected, so that the remedy itself healed the breach. The dictionary commends such wisdom: the church orders its practical ministries not only efficiently but justly and tenderly, that all things be done decently and in order (1 Cor 14:40) and that no group among God's people be overlooked or aggrieved.

etymology: Greek Timon, "honorable, esteemed"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6.
biblical_def: Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily ministration to the widows (Acts 6:5). His name means "honorable," and though Scripture records nothing of him beyond his place in the list, his appointment shines with quiet dignity. The Seven were the church's answer to a real and pressing need — the danger that, as the number of disciples multiplied, some of the needy would be overlooked. By appointing honorable, Spirit-filled men to this service, the apostles ensured that the practical love of the church would not fail. It is striking that two of the Seven, Stephen and Philip, soon appear as a mighty witness and an evangelist; the diaconate did not confine its members to tables alone, but the faithful discharge of humble service became the seedbed of wider usefulness. Of Timon himself nothing more is known, yet his name is preserved forever in the inspired record. Timon stands in the dictionary as one of the Seven whose name God saw fit to record, a witness that faithful service in the church, however obscure, is honorable in the sight of God, who forgets no labor of love done for His people in His name.
webster_summary: One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the widows; his name means "honorable," and though Scripture records no more of him, his place in the inspired list witnesses that obscure, faithful service is honorable before God.

corruption_summary: Timon honors the recovery of the honor of obscure, faithful service, against a fame-seeking spirit that despises any ministry the world will not notice or applaud.
corruption_paragraphs: Obscurity-despised correction. A culture obsessed with recognition counts unnoticed service worthless. Timon is named once and never described, yet his name stands forever in the Word of God, and his service to the widows was dear to the Lord. The dictionary holds that God is not unrighteous to forget the labor of love shown toward His name (Heb 6:10); the obscure servant is seen, remembered, and honored by the One whose esteem outweighs all the applause of men.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness in small and hidden things. It is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Cor 4:2), not famous. The dictionary commends the example of the lesser-known of the Seven: the kingdom of God advances through multitudes of faithful, unremembered servants, and what is done for the least of Christ's brethren is done unto Him (Matt 25:40), and shall not lose its reward.

etymology: Greek Parmenas, perhaps "steadfast" or "abiding"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6.
biblical_def: Parmenas was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve the widows in the daily ministration (Acts 6:5). Like several of his fellows, he appears in Scripture only in the list of the Seven, his later life unrecorded. Yet the office to which he and the others were appointed marks a vital moment in the life of the church: the first formal provision of a servant-ministry to care for the practical needs of the body, that the apostles might give themselves "continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4). The result was striking: "the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly" (Acts 6:7). The orderly care of the needy and the freeing of the apostles for the Word went hand in hand with the gospel's advance. Parmenas's name, possibly meaning "steadfast," fittingly adorns a man set to a ministry requiring patient, abiding faithfulness. He stands in the dictionary as one of the Seven, a witness that the steadfast, unremembered servants of the church are essential to her health and growth, and that the humble ministry of mercy, faithfully discharged, clears the way for the multiplying of the Word of God.
webster_summary: One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the widows; named only in the list, yet part of the servant-ministry that freed the apostles for the Word, so that "the word of God increased" and the disciples multiplied.

corruption_summary: Parmenas and the Seven honor the recovery of the link between practical service and the spread of the Word, against a false spirituality that divorces mercy-ministry from the advance of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Service-versus-Word correction. Some pit practical mercy against the ministry of the Word, as though the church must choose between them. Acts 6 binds them together: the Seven were appointed to serve tables precisely so the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the Word, and the immediate result was that "the word of God increased" (Acts 6:7). The dictionary holds that orderly mercy-ministry and the faithful preaching of the Word are partners, not rivals; the one clears the way for the other, and both flourish together.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is steadfastness in the work of the Lord. Parmenas, whose name may mean "steadfast," was set to a ministry of patient, ongoing care. The dictionary commends the apostolic exhortation: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord" (1 Cor 15:58). The unseen, steadfast laborer's work is not in vain in the Lord, but bears fruit in the multiplying of disciples and the increase of the Word.

etymology: Greek Nikolaos, "victor of the people"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6, distinguished as "a proselyte of Antioch."
biblical_def: Nicolas was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve the widows (Acts 6:5), set apart in the list by the note that he was "a proselyte of Antioch" — that is, a Gentile who had first converted to Judaism and then come to faith in Christ. This small detail is significant: among the first servants of the church was a Gentile by birth, a foretaste of the gospel's reach beyond Israel that would soon burst forth at Antioch itself, where the disciples were first called Christians and the first great Gentile mission was launched. That a former Gentile proselyte should be entrusted with holy service shows the early breadth of the church's fellowship. Of Nicolas's later life Scripture says nothing. An ancient and disputed tradition linked his name to the "Nicolaitans" whose deeds Christ hated in the Revelation (Rev 2:6, 15), but Scripture neither makes nor warrants that connection, and the link is uncertain at best. Nicolas stands in the dictionary as the Gentile proselyte among the Seven, a quiet early witness that the gospel gathers servants from every people, and a caution that a name once honorable may be wrongly claimed by later error — for the faithfulness of a man is not measured by those who would later borrow his name.
webster_summary: One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5, noted as "a proselyte of Antioch" (a Gentile convert); an early witness to the gospel's reach beyond Israel, whose name a disputed later tradition wrongly linked to the Nicolaitans.

corruption_summary: Nicolas's note honors the recovery of the gospel's reach to every people, against a narrow exclusivism, while his disputed link to the Nicolaitans cautions against building doctrine on uncertain tradition.
corruption_paragraphs: Exclusivism correction. That a Gentile proselyte stood among the first servants of the Jerusalem church foreshadows the gospel's breaking forth to the nations. The dictionary holds the breadth of the new-covenant fellowship: in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Gal 3:28), and from the beginning the church drew its servants from every people, against any spirit that would confine the grace of God to one nation or kind.

Tradition-over-Scripture caution. An ancient guess connected Nicolas to the Nicolaitans whose deeds Christ hated; but Scripture makes no such link, and to assume it is to convict a man on rumor. The dictionary holds that doctrine and judgment must rest on the written Word, not on uncertain tradition; a name borrowed by later heretics does not stain the man who bore it first. We honor what Scripture says of Nicolas — that he was chosen, full of the Spirit, among the Seven — and refuse to read into his name what the text does not say.

etymology: Aramaic Barsabbas, "son of the Sabbath"; surnamed Justus; the disciple not chosen when Matthias was selected to replace Judas.
biblical_def: Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, was one of the two faithful men put forward to fill the apostolic office vacated by Judas, the one not chosen when the lot fell upon Matthias (Acts 1:23-26). His qualifications were the same as Matthias's: he had companied with the disciples from the baptism of John until the ascension, a witness of the resurrection. When the believers prayed and cast lots, "the lot fell upon Matthias," and Joseph was passed by. Scripture records no complaint, no bitterness, no departure; he had stood ready to serve, and when God's choice fell on another, he accepted it. His threefold name — Joseph, Barsabbas, Justus ("the just") — and his very nomination mark him as a man of standing and integrity among the brethren. Of his later life nothing is told. Joseph Barsabbas stands in the dictionary as the disciple not chosen, a quiet model of humble submission to the providence of God: a man qualified, willing, and overlooked, who did not grasp at office but rested in the Lord's appointment, teaching the church that faithfulness is proved as much in the place we are not given as in the place we are.
webster_summary: The disciple put forward with Matthias to replace Judas, but not chosen when the lot fell on Matthias (Acts 1:23-26); a model of humble submission to God's providence, qualified and willing yet content to be passed by.

corruption_summary: Joseph Barsabbas honors the recovery of humble submission to God's providence in being passed over, against an ambitious spirit that grasps at office and resents being overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Ambition correction. The natural heart grasps at honor and resents being passed by. Joseph Barsabbas, qualified and willing, was not chosen, yet Scripture records no protest from him. The dictionary holds the grace of contentment in God's appointment: the servant is to humble himself under the mighty hand of God, who exalts in due time (1 Pet 5:6), and to trust that the Lord who knows all hearts places each where He wills. Faithfulness does not demand a particular office; it rests in the will of God.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness in being overlooked. Joseph stood ready to serve as an apostle, and when another was chosen, he did not abandon the church or sulk; he remained among the brethren. The dictionary commends his example: many are called to serve in places they did not choose, or to be passed over for honors they were fit to bear, and the godly response is not envy but glad submission to the wise providence of God, who forgets no faithful servant.

etymology: A chief man among the brethren at Jerusalem, sent with Silas to carry the decree of the Jerusalem Council to Antioch (Acts 15).
biblical_def: Judas Barsabbas was a leading member of the Jerusalem church, chosen with Silas to carry the decision of the Jerusalem Council to the Gentile believers at Antioch. When the council had settled the great question of whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses — ruling that they need not, but should abstain from certain things — they did not merely send a letter, but sent "chosen men of their own company," namely "Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren" (Acts 15:22), to deliver and confirm it in person. The letter named them as men "that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Acts 15:26). At Antioch they read the decree, and being "prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them" (Acts 15:32). The choice was wise: the gracious decision was carried not by a cold document but by trusted, gifted men who could explain it, encourage the church, and embody the unity it expressed. Judas Barsabbas stands in the dictionary as the trusted messenger of the council, a witness that the church guards its unity not only by right decisions but by sending faithful men to deliver them with grace, that the truth might be received with confidence and the brethren confirmed and encouraged.
webster_summary: A chief man of the Jerusalem church, sent with Silas to carry the Jerusalem Council's decree to Antioch (Acts 15:22-32); a prophet who, with Silas, confirmed and encouraged the Gentile believers with many words.

corruption_summary: Judas Barsabbas honors the recovery of the personal, gracious delivery of the church's decisions and the ministry of encouragement, against a cold institutionalism that issues decrees without shepherding hearts.
corruption_paragraphs: Cold-decree correction. The church might have settled the Gentile question with a bare letter; instead it sent trusted men to deliver it by mouth, explain it, and encourage the believers. The dictionary holds that truth is to be conveyed not only correctly but pastorally: the council sent prophets who exhorted the brethren with many words and confirmed them (Acts 15:32). Right decisions need faithful messengers who shepherd the hearts of those who receive them, that the truth may bring not confusion but consolation and joy.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ministry of encouragement and confirmation. Judas and Silas did not merely inform; they strengthened. The dictionary commends this work: the church abounds with believers who are wavering, weary, or unsure, and God gives gifted men to exhort them with many words and confirm them in the faith. To establish and encourage the brethren is a true and needed ministry, and the church is poorer where it is neglected.

etymology: A prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1), from Cyrene in North Africa.
biblical_def: Lucius of Cyrene was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, named among the leaders who were ministering to the Lord and fasting when the Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for the first great missionary journey. "Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen... and Saul" (Acts 13:1). The list is striking for its diversity: a Levite from Cyprus (Barnabas), a man called Niger ("black"), Lucius from Cyrene in North Africa, Manaen who had been raised with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul of Tarsus — men of varied background, race, and station, united in the leadership of the church. As they worshiped and fasted, the Spirit spoke, and they sent forth Barnabas and Saul, beginning the deliberate mission to the Gentiles. Cyrene, Lucius's home, had already given Simon who bore the cross and men who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11:20). Lucius stands in the dictionary as one of the diverse leaders of the church at Antioch, a witness that the gospel gathers its teachers from every nation, and that the great mission to the world was launched by a praying, fasting church listening for the voice of the Spirit.
webster_summary: A prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1), from Cyrene in North Africa; among the diverse leaders who, fasting and worshiping, sent out Barnabas and Saul when the Spirit set them apart for the first missionary journey.

corruption_summary: Lucius and the Antioch leaders honor the recovery of the gospel's gathering of teachers from every nation and the launching of missions from a worshiping, praying church, against both a narrow ethnocentrism and a missions divorced from prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: Ethnocentrism correction. The leadership at Antioch was strikingly diverse — a Cypriot Levite, a man called Niger, an African from Cyrene, a man raised in Herod's court, and a Pharisee of Tarsus. The dictionary holds that the gospel gathers its servants from every nation and station, uniting them in Christ; the unity of the church is not the erasure of difference but its reconciliation under one Lord, and the Antioch church witnesses that God raises up teachers from peoples far and near.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is missions born in worship and prayer. The first deliberate sending of missionaries came not from a committee's strategy but from a church ministering to the Lord and fasting, when the Spirit spoke. The dictionary commends the pattern: the great work of missions is the Spirit's, set in motion among a praying, worshiping people who listen for His voice and obey, sending out their best with fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands.

etymology: Greek Iason; the believer at Thessalonica who hosted Paul and Silas and was dragged before the rulers for it (Acts 17).
biblical_def: Jason was a believer at Thessalonica who lodged Paul and Silas during their brief, fruitful, and turbulent ministry there, and who paid a price for his hospitality. When the gospel took hold and many believed, certain unbelieving Jews, "moved with envy," gathered a mob and assaulted the house of Jason, seeking Paul and Silas to bring them out to the people (Acts 17:5). Not finding them, "they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also; whom Jason hath received" (Acts 17:6-7). The charge was that they acted contrary to Caesar's decrees, saying there is another king, one Jesus. The rulers, troubled, "took security of Jason, and of the other, and... let them go" (Acts 17:9) — that is, Jason posted a bond, likely guaranteeing the missionaries' departure, and so the brethren sent Paul and Silas away by night. Jason stands in the dictionary as the host who suffered for sheltering the gospel's messengers, a witness to the cost and the dignity of Christian hospitality, and to the world's enduring complaint against the gospel — that it turns the world upside down and proclaims another King, one Jesus, before whom even Caesar must bow.
webster_summary: The Thessalonian believer who hosted Paul and Silas (Acts 17:5-9); dragged before the rulers and made to post bond when a mob accused the missionaries of "turning the world upside down" and proclaiming another king, Jesus.

Acts 17:6

Acts 17:9

corruption_summary: Jason honors the recovery of costly Christian hospitality and of the gospel's claim that Jesus is King above Caesar, against a privatized faith that risks nothing and denies Christ's lordship over the public realm.
corruption_paragraphs: Risk-free hospitality correction. A comfortable religion offers hospitality only when it costs nothing. Jason opened his home to the messengers of the gospel and was dragged before the rulers and made to post bond for it. The dictionary holds that Christian hospitality may be costly and even dangerous, and is honorable still; to receive and shelter the servants of Christ, bearing the risk, is to share in their work and their reward, as Jason shared in the sufferings of Paul and Silas.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the public lordship of Christ. The charge against the brethren was that they proclaimed "another king, one Jesus," contrary to Caesar's decrees. The gospel was rightly understood by its enemies to make a kingly claim. The dictionary holds that Christ is King over all, including the powers of this world; the faith is not a private opinion but the proclamation that Jesus reigns, and the world still complains, as at Thessalonica, that such preaching turns its order upside down.
